procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court (inferred from the text 'judgments of the Trial Court and High Court')
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 26.11.2014 of the High Court of Madras at Madurai in CRLA No.240 of 2014
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Madras at Madurai issued a Judgment and Order dated 26.11.2014 in CRLA No.240 of 2014.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The present appeals (Criminal Appeal No. 270 of 2019 and Criminal Appeal No. 271 of 2019) are a challenge to the judgments of the Trial Court and High Court. The Supreme Court heard arguments from counsel for the appellants (A-1 and A-2) and the respondent (the State). The appeals were allowed.

directions: Both appellants are directed to be released forthwith, if not required in any other case.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in affirming the judgment of the trial court convicting and sentencing accused appellant (A-1) for the offence punishable under sections 302 & 307 of the Penal Code, 1860 and accused appellant (A-2) for the offence punishable under sections 302/109 & 307/109 of the Penal Code, 1860.

facts: The trial court convicted accused appellant (A-1) for murder (Section 302 IPC) and attempted murder (Section 307 IPC), and accused appellant (A-2) for abetting these offences (Sections 302/109 & 307/109 IPC).
The conviction was based on ocular (eyewitness) and medical evidence.
The High Court, in an appeal, confirmed the conviction and sentence handed down by the trial court.
The appellants then appealed to the Supreme Court.
law: The core legal principle applied by the Supreme Court is that the prosecution must establish its case against the accused "beyond a reasonable doubt" to warrant a conviction.
application: The Supreme Court re-examined the evidence, particularly the testimonies of the eyewitnesses (PW-1, PW-2, and PW-3) that the lower courts had relied upon.

The Court identified significant flaws in the prosecution's case, including an unspecified "delay" and a "significant gap in the examination of PW-2," which it found rendered the circumstances questionable.
Due to these inconsistencies and weaknesses, the Court determined that the eyewitness testimonies were unreliable.
As the eyewitness evidence was deemed untrustworthy for both the murder and attempted murder charges, the Court held that the prosecution had failed to meet its burden of proof.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution had failed to establish its case against the accused appellants beyond a reasonable doubt. Consequently, it ruled that the High Court was not justified in affirming the trial court's judgment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the convictions and sentences for both appellants, and ordered their immediate release.

issue.issue_text: Whether the convictions handed down to A-1 and A-2 were based on the standard of beyond reasonable doubt having been met and, therefore, sustainable.

facts: The Trial Court convicted A-1 for the murder of two individuals and A-2 for abetting the murder of one of them, relying on the testimonies of three witnesses (PW-1, PW-2, and PW-3).
The High Court confirmed the convictions and sentences handed down by the Trial Court.
The Supreme Court was then tasked with determining if these convictions were sustainable and met the standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
law: The standard of proof required to sustain a criminal conviction is that the prosecution's case must be proven "beyond reasonable doubt".
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the record and identified "various lapses" in the prosecution's case.
It found that the testimonies of the injured witnesses and the Investigation Officer were not "inspiring confidence".
The Court determined that these lapses cumulatively affected the "overall sanctity of the prosecution case," causing it to be "shaken beyond a point" where a conviction could be considered just.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution's case fell short of the threshold of being proven beyond a reasonable doubt. As a result, the Court found that the convictions of A-1 and A-2 were not sustainable and could not be upheld.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in affirming the judgment of the trial court convicting and sentencing accused appellant (A-1) for the offence punishable under sections 302 & 307 of the Penal Code, 1860 and accused appellant (A-2) for the offence punishable under sections 302/109 & 307/109 of the Penal Code, 1860.
appellant_arguments: The primary argument was for complete acquittal.

The prosecution's case was challenged on the grounds of: delay in lodging the FIR; almost all witnesses being 'interested witnesses'; a lack of independent witnesses; and the absence of enmity between the involved persons.
It was argued on behalf of A-2 that his presence at the scene of the crime was never established.
As a secondary submission, A-1 urged the right of private defence in the alternative to complete acquittal.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (the State) filed detailed submissions attempting to discredit all the arguments made on behalf of the accused persons.
The State relied on various judgments from the Supreme Court to support its case that the conviction was justified.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the convictions handed down to A-1 and A-2 were based on the standard of beyond reasonable doubt having been met and, therefore, sustainable.
appellant_arguments: The primary argument was for complete acquittal, implying the standard of 'beyond reasonable doubt' was not met.
The prosecution's case was challenged on several grounds: delay in lodging the FIR; the witnesses being 'interested witnesses'; a lack of independent witnesses; and no enmity between the parties.
A-2 specifically argued that his presence at the scene of the crime was not established.
As an alternative to acquittal, A-1 argued for the right of private defence.
respondent_arguments: The respondent attempted to discredit all submissions made by the appellants.
The State argued that the conviction, which was based on witness testimonies, was sound and met the required standard of proof, relying on various court judgments to support this position.

cases.case_name: Vidhya Singh v. State of M.P.
cases.principle: The right of private defence should not be construed narrowly.

cases.case_name: Rajesh and Anr. v. State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.principle: Cited for a remark made by a 3-Judge Bench while setting aside a conviction.

cases.case_name: Darshan Singh v. State of Punjab & Anr.
cases.principle: For the summarised principles in regard to the exercise of the right of private defence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Even if an accused individual does not formally plead self-defence, it is permissible for the court to consider such a plea if the evidence and material on record suggest its possibility.
obiter: The evidence of an injured witness is considered to be on a higher pedestal than that of a witness simpliciter.
It is not the law that the evidence of an interested witness should be equated with that of a tainted evidence or that of an approver so as to require corroboration as a matter of necessity.

Self-preservation is the basic human instinct and is duly recognised by the criminal jurisprudence of all civilised countries, which recognize the right of private defence within certain reasonable limits.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that numerous cumulative lapses affected the overall sanctity of the prosecution's case, causing it to fall short of the threshold of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. The court was unable to sustain the conviction because the testimony of the injured witnesses and the Investigation Officer was not confidence-inspiring, and the prosecution's case was shaken beyond a point where a conviction could be considered just. The specific grounds for sustaining the challenge to the conviction included: the examined private persons were interested witnesses with inconsistencies among them; no independent witnesses were examined; there was a delay in filing the FIR; there were interpolations on record; there were numerous lapses in the investigation; and the medical and scientific evidence did not support the prosecution’s version of events.
legal_tests_applied: The standard of proof in a criminal case is 'beyond reasonable doubt'.

As a rule of prudence, not a rule of law, the evidence of interested witnesses should be scrutinised with a little care. If the court is satisfied that the evidence of interested witnesses has a ring of truth, such evidence can be relied upon even without corroboration.
policy_considerations: The court recognizes that in some circumstances, such as an incident occurring at midnight within a house, only interested family members may be available as witnesses. In such cases, it would be improper to insist that their evidence be disbelieved merely because of their relationship to the parties involved, but prudence requires their testimony to be scrutinized with care.
